title: Compound Interest Growth Over Time
learningObjectives: Understand how the final amount is calculated with A=P*(1+r/(100*n))^(n*t) using the starting amount, annual rate, compounding frequency and time
Explain how changing the annual rate and time changes the final amount, similar to how different time scales affect change in physical systems
Apply the formula to predict amounts with yearly, quarterly and monthly compounding

explanations.text: A starting amount grows when interest is added repeatedly using A=P*(1+r/(100*n))^(n*t). P is the initial value before any growth is applied, similar to how new material builds up from a starting process over time.

evidence.quote: Plutonium is created in a reactor when uranium atoms absorb neutrons.

explanations.text: Time affects how much a quantity changes. Shorter and longer time scales produce different amounts of change, just as different half-lives describe different rates of transformation over years.

evidence.quote: Pu-239 has a half-life of 24,100 years and Pu-241’s half-life is 14.4 years.
Substances with shorter half-lives decay more quickly than those with longer half-lives, so they emit more energetic radioactivity.

explanations.text: Separation and mixing steps change what a final mixture contains. In compound interest, the principal and added interest mix over each period to form a new base for the next period of growth.

evidence.quote: This process, known as reprocessing, uses chemicals to separate plutonium from uranium and other fission products.
Once separated, plutonium oxide can be mixed with uranium oxide to produce mixed oxide or MOX fuel.
